items.name: Readability
items.evidence: The only deliverable is recovered.json, which reads cleanly. All the logic was throwaway inline `python3 -c` snippets with no named script or comments, and the key appears as a bare `b ^ 0x42` with no explanation.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: No decrypt or extract script is left behind to re-run; the fix was one long inline `python3 -c` command. Scratch files (orig_only.db, etc.) are left in an unrelated ~/.gemini/.../scratch directory. It is still small and has no copy-paste sprawl.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: The final step overwrites /app/main.db-wal with `bytes(b ^ 0x42 ...)` without checking for the 0x377f0682 magic. There is no error handling, and 0x42 is a hardcoded constant in that step. Nothing is silently swallowed, and the work was verified earlier.

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: The key was derived from the header (`0x753d44c0 ^ 0x42424242 == 0x377f0682`). The agent parsed the frame headers, let SQLite replay the WAL, ran `integrity_check: ok`, compared against the base DB (5 rows), and confirmed 11 rows.

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: The originals were copied to scratch first, but step 3 decrypted that copy in place and SQLite checkpointed it away (step 4 lists only main.db). After that, /app/main.db-wal was overwritten in place, so no copy of the encrypted WAL is left. It was decrypted before opening, so no data was lost.
